questions.stem: Review the data in the client's record. Highlight the findings that require follow-up by the nurse.

cells: ST depression and T-wave inversion in V4 to V6

rationale.correct: The cues that matter are those showing infarction (ECG, rising troponin) and those that change the safety of treatment (kidney function with metformin and contrast, daily NSAID use).

perOption.r1: ST depression with T-wave inversion shows subendocardial ischemia; with rising troponin it is an NSTEMI.
perOption.r2: A rising troponin confirms ongoing myocardial cell death, not stable angina.
perOption.r3: Current ACS guidance gives oxygen only when SpO2 is below 90%; 93% does not need oxygen.
perOption.r4: Reduced kidney function plus iodinated contrast raises the risk of contrast-associated kidney injury, and metformin then risks lactic acidosis.
perOption.r5: NSAIDs raise the risk of further cardiovascular events and bleeding with antiplatelets, and harm the kidneys.
perOption.r7: Normal; a baseline count before heparin, not a problem now.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the cues of NSTEMI and of procedure risk.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate what it shows about the client's condition.

rows.text: Chest pressure at rest for 2 hours
Troponin rising from 0.9 to 2.4 ng/mL in 2 hours
Chest pain falling from 6 to 4 of 10 after treatment began

columns.text: Raises risk from the planned treatment

rationale.correct: Analysis separates the evidence for the diagnosis (rest pain, rising troponin) from factors that make the treatment itself risky (kidney disease and NSAID use before contrast and antithrombotics).

perOption.r1:c1: Pain at rest lasting more than 20 minutes is acute coronary syndrome, not stable angina.
perOption.r1:c2: Pain at rest lasting more than 20 minutes is acute coronary syndrome, not stable angina.
perOption.r1:c3: Pain at rest lasting more than 20 minutes is acute coronary syndrome, not stable angina.
perOption.r2:c1: A rise in troponin separates NSTEMI (cell death) from unstable angina (no cell death).
perOption.r2:c2: A rise in troponin separates NSTEMI (cell death) from unstable angina (no cell death).
perOption.r2:c3: A rise in troponin separates NSTEMI (cell death) from unstable angina (no cell death).
perOption.r3:c1: Baseline kidney disease is the strongest risk factor for kidney injury after iodinated contrast.
perOption.r3:c2: Baseline kidney disease is the strongest risk factor for kidney injury after iodinated contrast.
perOption.r3:c3: Baseline kidney disease is the strongest risk factor for kidney injury after iodinated contrast.
perOption.r4:c1: With aspirin, heparin and later a P2Y12 inhibitor, NSAIDs add bleeding risk and reduce kidney blood flow.
perOption.r4:c2: With aspirin, heparin and later a P2Y12 inhibitor, NSAIDs add bleeding risk and reduce kidney blood flow.
perOption.r4:c3: With aspirin, heparin and later a P2Y12 inhibitor, NSAIDs add bleeding risk and reduce kidney blood flow.
perOption.r5:c1: Some relief is expected with treatment; it does not rule out infarction, so the plan continues.
perOption.r5:c2: Some relief is expected with treatment; it does not rule out infarction, so the plan continues.
perOption.r5:c3: Some relief is expected with treatment; it does not rule out infarction, so the plan continues.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze cues in a client with NSTEMI and procedure risk factors.

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: Before catheterization, the client's priority problem is {{b1}}, shown most clearly by {{b2}}. After the catheterization, the nurse should be most alert for {{b3}} because of {{b4}}.

options.text: the rising troponin with ST depression
the blood pressure of 158/94 mm Hg
the creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL with diabetes and daily NSAID use

rationale.correct: The first priority is ongoing ischemia; the next predictable danger is contrast-associated kidney injury in a client with CKD, diabetes and NSAID use.

perOption.b1:a: Rest pain with ST depression and rising troponin is active ischemia.
perOption.b1:b: There are no crackles, edema or hypoxemia below 90% to support it.
perOption.b1:c: Pericarditis gives diffuse ST elevation and pain that changes with position.
perOption.b1:d: A blood pressure of 158/94 is high but not in the emergency range.
perOption.b2:a: These show the infarction is evolving.
perOption.b2:b: Raised pressure adds workload but does not prove ischemia.
perOption.b2:c: Stress hyperglycemia is common and needs treatment, but it is not the evidence of ischemia.
perOption.b2:d: A mild rise in rate is not specific to ischemia.
perOption.b3:a: Contrast plus baseline kidney disease, diabetes and NSAIDs make kidney injury the key risk.
perOption.b3:b: Possible, but nothing in the history points to a contrast allergy.
perOption.b3:c: The client's glucose is high, and metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia.
perOption.b3:d: Iodine-induced thyroid problems are rare and late.
perOption.b4:a: Each of these lowers kidney reserve before the contrast load.
perOption.b4:b: Tachycardia does not predict kidney injury from contrast.
perOption.b4:d: Smoking raises coronary risk, not contrast kidney injury.

questions.stem: The provider writes the prescriptions shown. For each prescription, indicate whether it is indicated, not indicated, or contraindicated for the client at this time.

rows.text: Unfractionated heparin by weight-based bolus and infusion
Oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula
Ketorolac 30 mg IV for knee pain
Furosemide 40 mg IV before the contrast study

rationale.correct: Indicated: chewed aspirin, heparin and a high-intensity statin. Not indicated: oxygen above 90% and diuretics for kidney protection. Contraindicated: NSAIDs, and metformin around contrast with reduced kidney function.

perOption.r1:c1: Chewed aspirin acts fastest and reduces death in acute coronary syndrome.
perOption.r1:c2: Chewed aspirin acts fastest and reduces death in acute coronary syndrome.
perOption.r1:c3: Chewed aspirin acts fastest and reduces death in acute coronary syndrome.
perOption.r2:c1: Anticoagulation limits clot growth until the coronary anatomy is known.
perOption.r2:c2: Anticoagulation limits clot growth until the coronary anatomy is known.
perOption.r2:c3: Anticoagulation limits clot growth until the coronary anatomy is known.
perOption.r3:c1: With SpO2 at 93 to 94%, extra oxygen gives no benefit and may cause vasoconstriction.
perOption.r3:c2: With SpO2 at 93 to 94%, extra oxygen gives no benefit and may cause vasoconstriction.
perOption.r3:c3: With SpO2 at 93 to 94%, extra oxygen gives no benefit and may cause vasoconstriction.

perOption.r4:c2: NSAIDs raise the risk of reinfarction and bleeding and worsen kidney function before contrast.
perOption.r4:c3: NSAIDs raise the risk of reinfarction and bleeding and worsen kidney function before contrast.
perOption.r5:c1: Metformin is held on the day of contrast and for 48 hours after in a client with reduced kidney function, until creatinine is rechecked, because of the risk of lactic acidosis.
perOption.r5:c2: Metformin is held on the day of contrast and for 48 hours after in a client with reduced kidney function, until creatinine is rechecked, because of the risk of lactic acidosis.
perOption.r5:c3: Metformin is held on the day of contrast and for 48 hours after in a client with reduced kidney function, until creatinine is rechecked, because of the risk of lactic acidosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate solutions for NSTEMI, including drugs to hold.

exhibits.title: Prescriptions, 0930
exhibits.body: Aspirin 324 mg chewed now. Heparin 60 units/kg IV bolus, then 12 units/kg/hour. Oxygen 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Ketorolac 30 mg IV every 6 hours as needed for knee pain. Continue metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. Furosemide 40 mg IV before the contrast study. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily.

questions.stem: Review the 1530 update. Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion and call the provider
Apply firm pressure just above the puncture site
Keep the client flat with the right leg straight
Give IV 0.9% sodium chloride as a bolus as prescribed
Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees to ease back pain
Give the prescribed morphine for the back pain first
Recheck the hemoglobin in 4 hours before calling the provider

rationale.correct: Retroperitoneal bleeding shows as back or flank pain, hypotension and tachycardia with a clean groin dressing. Stop anticoagulants, compress above the puncture, keep the leg straight, support volume and call the provider.

perOption.a: Back pain with falling pressure and hemoglobin after femoral access is a retroperitoneal bleed; anticoagulation stops.
perOption.b: Pressure over the femoral artery above the skin puncture compresses the arterial entry point, where the bleeding starts.
perOption.c: Flexing the hip can reopen the arterial puncture; flat positioning also supports perfusion.
perOption.d: Isotonic fluid supports perfusion while blood is typed and crossmatched.
perOption.e: Hip flexion increases bleeding from the femoral artery.
perOption.f: Opioids lower blood pressure further and hide the sign that tracks the bleed.
perOption.g: Hemoglobin lags behind blood loss; the vital signs already show shock developing.

perOption.r1:c2: Pressure and rate have recovered, so blood loss has slowed and volume has been restored.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate outcomes after a retroperitoneal bleed and contrast exposure.

questions.stem: Review the nurses' notes. Highlight the findings that are most likely related to the client's medications.

segments.text: A 78-year-old client with heart failure is admitted with
4 days of nausea and poor appetite
seeing yellow and rings around lights
1+ ankle edema that the client says is usual
62 kg, down 2 kg in a week

rationale.correct: Gastrointestinal, visual and neurologic symptoms with slow pulse and ectopy fit digoxin toxicity, made worse by diuretic volume loss.

perOption.s2: Anorexia and nausea are early signs of digoxin toxicity.
perOption.s4: Yellow-green vision and halos are classic for digoxin toxicity.
perOption.s6: Confusion in an older adult is a common sign of digoxin toxicity.
perOption.s8: A stable baseline finding of chronic heart failure.
perOption.s10: Clear lungs argue against fluid overload; not a drug effect.
perOption.s12: Weight loss after the furosemide increase points to volume depletion, which concentrates digoxin.
perOption.s14: Bradycardia and ventricular ectopy are cardiac signs of digoxin toxicity.

questions.stem: For each factor, indicate how it contributes to the client's digoxin toxicity.

columns.text: Makes the heart more sensitive to digoxin

rationale.correct: Toxicity comes from a higher level (drug interaction, kidney decline) and a more sensitive heart (low potassium and magnesium, beta blockade).

perOption.r1:c1: Clarithromycin blocks P-glycoprotein and reduces digoxin clearance, so the level rises.
perOption.r1:c2: Clarithromycin blocks P-glycoprotein and reduces digoxin clearance, so the level rises.
perOption.r1:c3: Clarithromycin blocks P-glycoprotein and reduces digoxin clearance, so the level rises.
perOption.r2:c1: Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys; reduced kidney function lets it build up.
perOption.r2:c2: Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys; reduced kidney function lets it build up.
perOption.r2:c3: Digoxin is cleared by the kidneys; reduced kidney function lets it build up.
perOption.r3:c1: Low potassium lets more digoxin bind to the sodium-potassium pump, increasing toxicity at any level.
perOption.r3:c2: Low potassium lets more digoxin bind to the sodium-potassium pump, increasing toxicity at any level.
perOption.r3:c3: Low potassium lets more digoxin bind to the sodium-potassium pump, increasing toxicity at any level.

perOption.r4:c2: Low magnesium also increases the heart's sensitivity and the risk of dysrhythmia.
perOption.r4:c3: Low magnesium also increases the heart's sensitivity and the risk of dysrhythmia.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate solutions for digoxin toxicity.

exhibits.title: Prescriptions, 1100
exhibits.body: Hold digoxin. Potassium chloride 40 mEq IV at 10 mEq/hour. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1 hour. Furosemide 40 mg IV now. Continue clarithromycin. Fluid restriction 1.5 L/day. Atropine 1 mg at the bedside. Continuous cardiac monitoring.

questions.stem: At 1400, the client has a 7-beat run of ventricular tachycardia and the apical pulse falls to 38/min with BP 80/48 mm Hg. The provider prescribes digoxin immune fab. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give the digoxin immune fab over 30 minutes through a filter as prescribed
Place transcutaneous pacing pads on the client
Recheck potassium within 1 to 2 hours after the dose
Draw a digoxin level 1 hour after the dose to judge its effect
Prepare for synchronized cardioversion at 200 joules
Give the 1200 dose of carvedilol now

rationale.correct: Give the antidote, be ready to pace, and watch potassium closely because it falls as fab works. Serum levels after fab are misleading.

perOption.a: Fab fragments bind digoxin and reverse life-threatening toxicity within an hour.
perOption.b: Severe bradycardia with hypotension may need pacing until the antidote works.
perOption.c: As the pump is freed, potassium moves back into cells, so hypokalemia can worsen quickly.
perOption.d: Most tests measure bound plus free digoxin after fab, so the level rises falsely; judge by the rhythm and symptoms.
perOption.e: Cardioversion in digoxin toxicity can trigger ventricular fibrillation; it is not the first step.
perOption.f: A beta blocker would slow the heart further.

questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are most important for planning the client's care.

cells: Irregularly irregular, no P waves, rate 148/min

rationale.correct: The key cues are the rhythm, how long it has lasted, the stroke risk and the thyroid cause.

perOption.r1: This is atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate.
perOption.r2: AF lasting 48 hours or longer may already have formed an atrial clot, which changes how rhythm is restored.
perOption.r3: Prior TIA, hypertension, diabetes and age give a high stroke risk, so anticoagulation is needed.
perOption.r4: Thyrotoxicosis is a reversible cause of the AF and must be treated for rate control to work.
perOption.r7: A normal ejection fraction is reassuring; it allows a calcium channel blocker for rate control.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues in new atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: The client's shortness of breath is best explained by {{b1}}. Because the AF began more than 48 hours ago, restoring sinus rhythm now would raise the risk of {{b2}}. The thyroid results suggest the AF is {{b3}}.

options.text: a short filling time that lowers cardiac output
a pulmonary embolism from the atrial clot

rationale.correct: AF with rapid rate lowers output through short filling and lost atrial kick; after 48 hours, cardioversion risks stroke; thyrotoxicosis is the driver.

perOption.b1:a: At 148/min the ventricles have little time to fill, and the atrial kick is lost, so output falls and pressure backs up.
perOption.b1:b: Clots from the left atrium go to the systemic circulation, not the lungs.
perOption.b2:a: A clot formed in the fibrillating atrium can be thrown out when organized contraction returns.
perOption.b2:b: Not the main risk of restoring rhythm after 48 hours.
perOption.b3:a: Excess thyroid hormone raises sympathetic tone and atrial irritability; weight loss, heat and tremor fit.
perOption.b3:b: A TIA is a consequence of AF, not a cause.
perOption.b3:c: The weight loss is part of the thyrotoxic picture.

questions.stem: Review the 1745 findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed and raise the legs
Notify the provider of the blood pressure and rhythm
Give the IV fluid bolus prescribed for hypotension
Raise the diltiazem to 15 mg/hour to keep the rate below 100
Give the client's evening dose of amlodipine

questions.stem: The client is ready for discharge on apixaban, metoprolol and methimazole. For each statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs more teaching.

rows.text: "I will need regular INR blood tests to adjust my apixaban dose."

questions.stem: Review the nurses' notes. Highlight the findings that show damage to a target organ.

segments.text: a severe headache with blurred vision
is oriented to person and place only
2.0 mg/dL, double the value 6 months ago
protein and red cells in the urine

rationale.correct: Hypertensive emergency is defined by acute target-organ damage: brain (encephalopathy, papilledema), kidney (rising creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria) or heart.

perOption.s2: Headache with visual change reflects cerebral and retinal effects of severe pressure.
perOption.s6: Papilledema shows raised intracranial pressure or retinal damage.
perOption.s8: Common with clonidine rebound; a symptom, not organ damage.
perOption.s10: An acute rise in creatinine shows kidney injury.
perOption.s12: These point to acute kidney damage from severe pressure.
perOption.s14: Tachycardia fits clonidine rebound but is not evidence of organ damage by itself.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: This is hypertensive {{b1}} because {{b2}}, and the most likely trigger is {{b3}}.

perOption.b3:b: Twice-weekly albuterol does not explain this.

exhibits.title: Plan, 2230
exhibits.body: Nicardipine infusion. Labetalol 20 mg IV push. Goal: mean arterial pressure down by no more than 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours. Arterial line. Nifedipine 10 mg sublingual.

questions.stem: Review the 2330 findings. The nicardipine was increased twice by the night nurse. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decrease the nicardipine following the titration protocol
Perform a neurologic assessment, including a stroke scale
Notify the provider of the change
Keep the head of the bed flat or low to support brain perfusion
Give the client's home clonidine dose now
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees
Continue the current rate and recheck in an hour

rationale.correct: Lowering pressure too fast can cause brain ischemia. Reduce the drug, assess neurologically, support perfusion and call the provider.

perOption.a: Pressure has fallen too far, too fast; the infusion is reduced to stop the fall.
perOption.b: New slurred speech and drowsiness suggest brain hypoperfusion or stroke.
perOption.c: A new neurologic deficit needs urgent review and imaging.
perOption.d: This helps cerebral blood flow while pressure is corrected, unless aspiration risk prevents it.
perOption.g: A neurologic change needs action now.

caseStudies.title: NSTEMI with a retroperitoneal bleed after catheterization

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0700
exhibits.body: A 67-year-old client reports pressure in the center of the chest at rest for the past 2 hours, with sweating and shortness of breath. History: type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3, hypertension, 40 pack-years of smoking. Home medications: metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 10 mg daily, and over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for knee pain. The 12-lead ECG shows 2 mm ST depression and T-wave inversion in V4 to V6. Cardiac catheterization is planned for this afternoon.

exhibits.title: Medical unit admission, 1000
exhibits.body: A 78-year-old client with heart failure (ejection fraction 25%) and chronic atrial fibrillation is admitted with 4 days of nausea, poor appetite and fatigue. The client says, "Everything looks yellow, and there are rings around the lights." The client's daughter reports new confusion since yesterday. Furosemide was increased from 40 mg daily to 40 mg twice daily 10 days ago, and clarithromycin was started 5 days ago for bronchitis. Other medications: digoxin 0.25 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily. Lungs clear, 1+ ankle edema (the client says this is usual), weight 62 kg (64 kg one week ago). Monitor: slow atrial fibrillation with frequent premature ventricular contractions.

rows.label: Digoxin
cells: 0.5 to 2.0 ng/mL (0.5 to 0.9 in heart failure)

caseStudies.title: New atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate from thyrotoxicosis

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 1600
exhibits.body: A 62-year-old client reports a racing heart and shortness of breath that began "three or four days ago." The client has lost 5 kg in 2 months without trying, feels hot, and has a fine tremor of the hands. History: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, a transient ischemic attack 2 years ago. An echocardiogram last year showed an ejection fraction of 55%. Home medications: amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily. The monitor shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no visible P waves.

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 2200
exhibits.body: A 54-year-old client reports a severe headache since this morning and blurred vision. The client ran out of clonidine 0.2 mg twice daily 2 days ago and "didn't think it mattered." History: hypertension for 15 years, asthma (uses an albuterol inhaler twice a week). The client is restless and slow to answer questions, and is oriented to person and place only. Fundoscopic examination by the provider shows papilledema. The client is sweating and anxious.
